title: Component Migration Playbook & Contribution Guide for Tokens and Primitives
creator: Ava Martinez
description: A single, pragmatic playbook that defines how designers and engineers contribute changes to core visual tokens and components (buttons, tables, charts, inputs). This doc codifies the RFC process for API/prop changes, the contribution checklist, automated checks (linting, visual snapshots), codemod strategy for migrations, and a safe deprecation cadence with compatibility wrappers and dual-run strategy.
review_checklist: Design spec attached with dos and don'ts (link to figma)
Accessibility audit pass (color contrast, keyboard, screen reader notes)
Token mapping table showing old -> new token names and values
Backward-compatibility plan: prop aliases or wrapper components
Performance impact analysis for tables/charts (render & bundle size)
Unit and visual regression tests included (storybook snapshots)
Codemod plan with sample transforms and dry-run metrics
Rollout strategy: canary component flag + telemetry points to monitor
Docs/Playground updated with migration examples and known gotchas
Security & privacy considerations reviewed if component affects telemetry
migration_timeline: Phase 0: Proposal + RFC (2 weeks) - gather stakeholders and initial spec
Phase 1: Prototype + internal compatibility wrappers (3 weeks) - publish alpha package
Phase 2: Codemod + docs (2 weeks) - provide automated migration and samples
Phase 3: Canary rollout + telemetry (4 weeks) - observe errors and adoption
Phase 4: Deprecation window (90 days after canary) - warn, then remove aliases
acceptance_criteria: At least one major consumer migrated with codemod applied successfully
No critical accessibility regressions in automated tests
Telemetry shows no >1% error rate attributed to migration after canary
Developer docs and example migration guides published
CI includes new lint rules and visual snapshot checks

notes: This playbook is intended to minimize friction for product teams adopting token and API changes. Key trade-offs: prefer short-lived compatibility wrappers to long-term API support to reduce maintenance cost; provide a generous deprecation window only for high-impact components. Cross-team sign-off required from Platform, SDK, and Accessibility leads before Phase 2.
